name: El Alto International Airport
before:
The highest international airport in the world, at 4,061 metres above sea level, and the seventh highest commercial airport anywhere. It is in the city of El Alto, 13 km west of La Paz and a good deal higher than it, so clients arrive at altitude before they have done anything at all. Build a gentle first day into any itinerary.

The terminal has shops selling Bolivian handicrafts, bookshops, duty free and cafes and restaurants in the main lobby and in both the domestic and international departure areas.

The airport has been in service since the first half of the twentieth century and was rebuilt in the late 1960s, with a lengthened runway and a new terminal opened in 1965.

It was the main hub for Lloyd Aereo Boliviano until the airline stopped flying in 2007, and is now a focus city for Boliviana de Aviacion, the state carrier.
after:
The highest airport with scheduled flights outside China, at more than 4,000 metres above sea level. It is in the city of El Alto, west of La Paz, so clients arrive at altitude before they have done anything at all. Build a gentle first day into any itinerary.

It has been in use since the first half of the twentieth century and was officially opened in 1965. Its terminal was modernised in the 2000s.

Boliviana de Aviación flies from here.

claims.claim: the highest airport with scheduled flights outside China
claims.inAfter: The highest airport with scheduled flights outside China
claims.note: Was 'the highest international airport in the world ... and the seventh highest commercial airport anywhere' (both cut below). OurAirports' data, read in full: of every airport it marks as having scheduled service, only five stand higher than El Alto, and all five are in China (Daocheng Yading, Qamdo Bangda, Shigatse Tingri, Kangding, Ngari Gunsa). Wikipedia says the same in its own words ('the highest commercial airport outside of China'). OurAirports does not say which airports have international flights, so 'international' is not kept.

claims.claim: the highest international airport in the world
claims.wasBefore: The highest international airport in the world
claims.why: 'International' rests on Wikipedia alone: OurAirports ranks the airports but does not say which have international flights, and no other readable source makes the claim (Airbus's high-altitude test pages are behind an Imperva bot check; AP is blocked by the egress policy). Softened to what both support (above).
Softened to 'more than 4,000 metres' (above): Wikipedia 4,061.5 m, OurAirports 4,071 m.

claims.wasBefore: and the seventh highest commercial airport anywhere
claims.why: The rank is disputed: Wikipedia says seventh, while OurAirports' data put it sixth among airports with scheduled service. The claim that nothing outside China is higher is kept (above).

claims.claim: 13 km west of La Paz and a good deal higher than it
claims.wasBefore: 13 km west of La Paz and a good deal higher than it
claims.why: 13 km fails the coordinates check (4.4 km in a straight line, ratio 2.99) and no written second source was found (the AIP site did not connect). 'A good deal higher' needs La Paz's own altitude from a second source; none was saved. The direction and the altitude advice are kept.

claims.claim: terminal shops, bookshops, duty free, cafes and restaurants
claims.wasBefore: The terminal has shops selling Bolivian handicrafts, bookshops, duty free and cafes and restaurants in the main lobby and in both the domestic and international departure areas.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone, and written about the 2006 rebuild; the operator's page lists free Wi-Fi, parking and taxi fares but no shops.

claims.claim: rebuilt in the late 1960s with a lengthened runway
claims.wasBefore: and was rebuilt in the late 1960s, with a lengthened runway and a new terminal opened in 1965
claims.why: Wikipedia alone, and it contradicts itself (a late-1960s rebuild, a 1965 opening and a 1974 reconstruction). The 1965 opening is kept (above) and the terminal's latest modernisation replaces the 'new terminal'.

claims.claim: main hub for Lloyd Aéreo Boliviano until 2007
claims.wasBefore: It was the main hub for Lloyd Aereo Boliviano until the airline stopped flying in 2007
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. Bolivia's DGAC history confirms LAB's founding in 1925 but not its hub or its end.

claims.claim: focus city for BoA, the state carrier
claims.wasBefore: is now a focus city for Boliviana de Aviacion, the state carrier
claims.why: Softened to 'flies from here' (above). 'Focus city' and 'the state carrier' rest on Wikipedia alone; BoA's site is behind a bot check and El Diario's report answered with a JavaScript challenge.

claims.claim: FCDO: State of Emergency; blockades can close roads to airports
claims.why: Held back, recommended for Andy: the FCDO (updated 22 September 2026) says a State of Emergency declared on 21 June gives police and the armed forces powers to remove roadblocks and disrupt protests, that protests may bring widespread road blockades including on roads to and from airports, and not to try to cross them. It also says altitude sickness is a risk in La Paz, which is the basis of the kept 'gentle first day' advice. Nothing in the old text to replace.

quote: A State of Emergency has been declared in Bolivia, giving police and armed forces powers to remove roadblocks, disrupt protests and detain those not complying with the new measures for up to 8 hours without charge.
A State of Emergency was declared in Bolivia on 21 June to restrict protests and blockades.
Protests or demonstrations may result in widespread road blockades, including on roads to and from airports.

sources.quote: Altitude sickness is a risk in parts of Bolivia, including in La Paz and the Salar de Uyuni salt flats.

claims.claim: Air Force C-130 overran the runway on 27 February 2026
claims.why: Held back, one source only: Wikipedia says a Bolivian Air Force C-130 Hercules overshot the runway on landing on 27 February 2026 and hit vehicles, killing at least 22 people. Its AP source is blocked by the egress policy and no Bolivian report was read. For Andy: probably not one for the Overview, but worth knowing.

sources.quote: On 27 February 2026, a C-130 Hercules aircraft of the Bolivian Air Force overshot the airport's runway during landing and collided with several vehicles, killing at least 22 people and injuring 29 others.

opinion.text: so clients arrive at altitude before they have done anything at all
opinion.why: Follows from the verified altitude (more than 4,000 metres); kept from the old text.

opinion.text: Build a gentle first day into any itinerary.
opinion.why: Advice kept from the old text. It rests on the verified altitude and on the FCDO's statement that altitude sickness is a risk in La Paz (held back entry above).
